system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2122-05-13 18:20:00 to 2122-05-16 15:00:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. Johnson, a patient with HCV-related cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma, and a history of GAVE-related bleeding, was admitted for dyspnea on exertion and lightheadedness due to anemia. His hemoglobin had dropped to 7.5 g/dL, likely from ongoing upper gastrointestinal blood loss related to GAVE. He received two units of packed red blood cells in the emergency department with improvement in symptoms and a rise in hemoglobin to 9.3 g/dL. Cardiac and pulmonary evaluations were unremarkable, and his chronic right upper quadrant pain was attributed to known intestinal malrotation. His cirrhosis remained stable without signs of decompensation. He was discharged home in stable condition with continued management of his liver disease, GAVE prophylaxis, and instructions to follow up with his liver specialist.
problems: Angiodysplasia of stomach and duodenum with hemorrhage
Cirrhosis of liver without mention of alcohol
Chronic hepatitis C without mention of hepatic coma

radiology_notes.text:
INDICATION:  ___ male patient with HCC, requiring pre-operative
evaluation for TACE.

COMPARISON:  Prior chest CT from ___ and chest radiograph from
___.

TECHNIQUE:  PA and lateral chest radiographs.

FINDINGS:  Low lung volumes accentuate the bronchovascular structures and
cardiac silhouette.  There is mild bibasilar atelectasis.  There are no focal
consolidations, pleural effusions or pneumothorax. There are rib deformities
on the right. 

IMPRESSION:  No radiographic evidence of an acute cardiopulmonary process.

INDICATION:  ___ man with ___, please perform chemoembolization of the
liver.

PHYSICIANS:  Dr. ___ (radiology fellow) and Dr. ___
___ (radiology attending) who was present throughout and supervised the
procedure.

MEDICATION:  The procedure was performed under moderate conscious sedation,
the patient received 2 mg of Versed and 150 mcg of fentanyl for the total
intraservice time of 135 minutes, during which time the patient's hemodynamic
parameters were continuously monitored.  In addition, the patient received 30
mg of Toradol IV.

For chemoembolization, the patient received 60 mg of doxorubicin mixed with 20
mL of Lipiodol and 10 mL of Optiray. 10cc of intrarterial lidocaine was
administered.

PROCEDURES:
1.  Right common femoral artery access.
2.  Right hepatic artery angiography.
3.  Right hepatic artery cone-beam CT angiography.
5.  Lipiodol/doxorubicin TACE to segment V/VI.

CONTRAST:  140 mL Optiray 320.

RADIATION:  1823 mGy, 43.5 minutes of fluoroscopy time.

PROCEDURE DETAILS:

Following discussion of the risks, benefits and alternatives to the procedure,
informed written patient consent was obtained.  The patient was brought to the
angiographic suite and placed supine on the table.  A preprocedure timeout was
performed using three patient identifiers.  The skin of the right groin was
prepped and draped in the usual sterile fashion.  

Approximately 5 cc of 1% lidocaine was infiltrated into the skin and
subcutaneous tissues for local anesthesia.  Using a combination of
fluoroscopic and palpatory guidance, a 21-gauge micropuncture needle was used
to access the common femoral artery.  An 018 nitinol wire was easily passed
through the needle which was then exchanged for a micropuncture sheath.  The
inner portion of the sheath and the wire were removed and exchanged for a
___ wire.  The micropuncture sheath was then exchanged for a 5 ___
___ Tip sheath, the sidearm which was continuously flushed with heparinized
saline throughout the procedure.  A 5 ___ C2 catheter was advanced over the
___ wire and positioned in the superior mesenteric artery.  SMA
angiography was performed at this point, which demonstrated a replaced right
hepatic artery arising directly from the SMA, the remainder of the mesenteric
branches were within normal limits. The portal vein was patent.  An 035
Glidewire was advanced through the C2 catheter into the replaced right hepatic
artery, the C2 catheter was removed and exchanged for a C2 glide catheter
which was positioned more distally in the right hepatic artery and repeat
angiography was performed.  This demonstrated two major branches within the
liver parenchyma, one passing superiorly towards the dome and one passing more
peripherally, this was accessed using a Glidewire and C2 catheter.  This
branch had two major branches within the liver parenchyma, both of these were
selectively accessed using a Fathom wire and Renegade ___ catheter. 
Contrast angiography performed in each of these vessels failed to demonstrate
a clear contrast blush indicating tumor supply; however a spin CT via the
right hepatic artery indicated that both vessels were supplying the region of
interest, therefore, we elected to perform chemoembolization via the main
trunk of this vessel, targeting segments V and VI.
A mixture of 60 mg of doxorubicin, 20 mL of Lipiodol and 10 mL of Optiray was
injected with intermittent injection of intra-arterial 1% lidocaine.  Once all
the doxorubicin had been administered, Gelfoam embolization was performed to
the trunk to near stasis.  The microcatheter and C2 catheter were removed.  An
angiographic run was performed at the access site demonstrating appropriate
level of access.  The sheath was removed and firm manual compression was
applied for 20 minutes, following which there was no further bleeding.  There
were no immediate post-procedure complications.

IMPRESSION:  
Technically successful semi selective chemoembolization of a segmental V/VI
branch of the right hepatic artery.
A mixture of 60 mg of doxorubicin, 20 mL of Lipiodol and 10 mL of Optiray was
injected.

HISTORY:  Status post TACE procedure.

TECHNIQUE:  CT of the abdomen without IV contrast.  Coronal and sagittal
reformats were reviewed.

COMPARISON:  MR from ___ and CT from ___.

FINDINGS:

The lung bases and cardiac apex are unremarkable.

Noncontrast appearance of the spleen, pancreas, bilateral kidneys and the
right adrenal is unremarkable.  The left adrenal is slightly obscured by large
splenic varices.  The stomach and imaged loops of large bowel as well as small
bowel are unremarkable.  Scattered abdominal lymphadenopathy is largely stable
from the prior exams.  The patient is status post cholecystectomy. Calcified
structure in the mid small bowel mesentery is stable and previously felt to
represent retained gallstones.

The patient is status post TACE with ethidiol uptake in the right lobe of the
liver including segment VII, VI and parts of V and VIII.   No extrahepatic
ethidiol uptake is demonstrated. The heterogenous appearance of the liver on
this non-contrast phase suggests underlying lesion, but is not fully
characterized here.

IMPRESSION:

Ethidiol uptake in the right lobe of the liver without evidence of
extrahepatic deposition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello Mr. Johnson, I'm Dr. Patel, one of your hospital doctors. You're here today after having a TACE procedure for your liver cancer. How are you feeling right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’m a bit sore in my right side, and I’ve got a mild headache. Also feel a little nauseous, but not bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s not uncommon after TACE. The pain in your right upper abdomen is expected—it’s from the treatment area. We’ll manage that with medications. Any fever, chest pain, or trouble breathing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, no chest pain or shortness of breath. Just the soreness and nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. You tolerated the procedure well according to the radiology team. They delivered chemotherapy directly to the tumor in your right liver lobe and blocked its blood supply. The imaging shows the medication reached the right spot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. But will the pain get worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It might increase a bit over the next day or two—that’s part of what we call ‘post-embolization syndrome.’ But we’ll keep you comfortable with pain meds like acetaminophen and, if needed, hydromorphone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. What about the nausea? Should I expect vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re giving you anti-nausea medications just in case—ondansetron and prochlorperazine. If it gets worse, we can add another one through your IV. Most patients feel better within a couple of days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright, that helps. My leg feels stiff—why the brace?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had the procedure through your right groin artery. The brace helps keep your leg straight to prevent bleeding at the access site. You’ll need to lie flat for several hours after the procedure, but you’re past that now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Any other risks I should know about?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re watching for infection, bleeding, or liver function changes. You’re on antibiotics just in case, and we’re checking blood work daily. Your liver enzymes might go up—that’s expected and usually temporary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I remember that from last time. My liver numbers went up before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. Johnson. I reviewed your labs. Your liver enzymes are elevated—AST and ALT are quite high, which we expected after TACE. They peaked this morning but should start coming down soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How high is high? Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: AST is 1225 and ALT is 527—much higher than normal, but this is a known reaction after TACE. It means the treated liver tissue is responding. We’ll keep monitoring them daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, as long as it’s expected. My stomach feels worse today—more nauseous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’ll order IV metoclopramide—that often helps when oral meds aren’t enough. Also, we’re giving you IV fluids to stay hydrated. Any vomiting yet?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, not yet. But I don’t want to eat anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s fine. You can stay on clear liquids today. We’ll advance your diet as you feel better. Your appetite should return in a day or two.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT scan from this morning shows good uptake of the treatment material in the right lobe of your liver. No spread outside the liver. That’s excellent news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great! So it went to the right place?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. The ethiodol is concentrated in segments V, VI, and parts of VII and VIII—right where we targeted. No signs of damage to other areas.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I’ve been having trouble urinating though—haven’t gone since yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s called urinary retention. It can happen after procedures, especially with pain meds. We may need to insert a catheter temporarily to help you empty your bladder.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I’d rather not, but if I have to… is it serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not serious—fairly common. We’ll try encouraging fluids and having you walk. If that doesn’t work, we’ll do a quick straight catheterization. It’s temporary and resolves quickly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We went ahead with a straight catheter—it drained over 800 mL. That’s a lot. You should feel better now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I already feel more comfortable. Thank you. Will I need it again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Unlikely. Now that your bladder has emptied, it should work normally. We’ll monitor, and you should be able to urinate on your own soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your nausea is better, and you kept down some toast. Liver enzymes are starting to come down—ALT is now 449, AST is 816. Still high, but trending in the right direction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. My pain is also less—only about a 4 now with the acetaminophen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. We’ll keep you on the hydromorphone just in case, but you’re doing well. Your platelets are lower than before—down to 44—so we’re watching for bleeding risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that because of the TACE?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely. Your liver disease already causes low platelets, and TACE can make it worse temporarily. We’ll avoid any medications that increase bleeding risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. What about my other labs? My phosphorus was low last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your phosphorus was 1.9, so we gave replacement. It’s now 2.0—still low normal, but improving. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Johnson, you’ve done really well. You’re eating, urinating on your own, pain is controlled, and labs are improving. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Fever and abdominal pain are common for a few days. Use acetaminophen first, and hydromorphone if needed. If you can’t urinate again, seek care right away. Also, watch for nosebleeds—use direct pressure if one happens.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my regular meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, resume all your home medications: lactulose, rifaximin, furosemide, spironolactone, nadolol, pantoprazole, mesalamine, and ciprofloxacin. We’re adding prochlorperazine for nausea if it returns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your liver specialist will see you in one week. We’ll also check your blood work soon to monitor liver function and platelets.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. You tolerated TACE well, and this treatment helps control your liver cancer. Rest, stay hydrated, and call if anything concerns you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. We’ll get your discharge papers ready. A nurse will go over the instructions one more time before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright, I appreciate it.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. Johnson was admitted for monitoring after undergoing his third transarterial chemoembolization (TACE) procedure for hepatocellular carcinoma. He tolerated the procedure well but developed expected post-embolization symptoms including right upper quadrant pain, nausea, and a significant transient elevation in liver enzymes. He also experienced temporary urinary retention requiring a straight catheterization, which resolved. His chronic conditions—alcoholic and hepatitis C-related cirrhosis, thrombocytopenia, and ulcerative colitis—were managed throughout the stay. Liver function tests peaked but began to improve, and symptoms were controlled with supportive care. He was discharged home in stable condition with updated medications and follow-up plans.
